chunks.title: HistoLens: overview
chunks.text: Classifies colorectal cancer tissue from microscope images into 9 tissue types. Trained on one hospital's slides, tested on 7,180 tiles from a different clinical center. Accuracy: 97.8% in training conditions (same hospital as training), 95.7% on match day (a different hospital). Stack: PyTorch, ResNet-18, ONNX Runtime, FastAPI, Streamlit. Demo: https://histolens.medouaishamdi.com. Code: https://github.com/medouaishamdi/histolens.

chunks.title: HistoLens: problem and approach
chunks.text: Pathologists classify tissue under the microscope to diagnose and grade colorectal cancer. Models that help them usually report accuracy on images from the same source they were trained on. Real deployments see slides from other labs, stained and scanned differently. HistoLens is trained on one center's slides and evaluated on another's. Compared four models under the same compute budget: a small CNN, ResNet-18 from scratch, and ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-18 with and without stain augmentation. Implemented H&E stain augmentation from scratch: colour deconvolution into hematoxylin, eosin and residual channels, random rescaling of each stain, then back to RGB. Measured calibration on the other hospital, tried temperature scaling, and added a referral threshold so uncertain tiles go to a human. Explained predictions with occlusion maps, and served the model with ONNX Runtime so the app needs no PyTorch.

chunks.title: HistoLens: lesson, Validation accuracy picks the wrong model
chunks.text: Without stain augmentation the pretrained ResNet scores 98.5% on same-hospital data, the best of all, but drops to 95.1% on the other hospital, behind even the small CNN.

chunks.title: HistoLens: lesson, Stain augmentation helps, modestly
chunks.text: On the other hospital it fixes 171 tiles and breaks 124 (+0.6 points, McNemar p = 0.007). One training run per model, so more seeds would be needed to claim more.

chunks.title: HistoLens: lesson, Referring uncertain cases pays off
chunks.text: Answering only the 90% most confident tiles raises accuracy from 95.7% to 98.7%.

chunks.title: HistoLens: limitations
chunks.text: Tiles, not whole slides: a clinical tool would aggregate thousands of tiles per patient. 64×64 pixels per tile and only two medical centers. No out-of-distribution check: a non-tissue image still gets one of the 9 labels. Research project on public data (PathMNIST), not a medical device.

chunks.title: WattCast: overview
chunks.text: Forecasts France's hourly electricity consumption one day ahead. Backtested over 7.5 years and compared hour by hour with RTE's official forecasts. Forecast error (MAPE, 2025): 1.89% error in training conditions (with observed temperatures), 2.4% error on match day (with realistic weather-forecast error). Stack: LightGBM, pandas, Conformal prediction, FastAPI, Streamlit. Demo: https://wattcast.medouaishamdi.com. Code: https://github.com/medouaishamdi/wattcast.

chunks.title: WattCast: problem and approach
chunks.text: Electricity can't be stored at scale, so every day RTE forecasts tomorrow's demand, hour by hour. Power plants are scheduled and electricity is traded on that forecast. WattCast does the same with public data: 11 years of RTE eCO2mix consumption and the temperature of five large French cities. Day-ahead setup: the forecast for day D is made on D-1, so only consumption up to D-2 is used. A test checks that no future data leaks into the features. Features for calendar effects (French holidays, bridge days, August), thermal inertia of buildings, and recent consumption. Expanding-window backtest: every year from 2019 to 2026 is forecast by a model trained only on the years before it. 80% prediction intervals made reliable with conformal calibration on a held-out year.

chunks.title: WattCast: lesson, RTE is still better, honestly
chunks.text: WattCast edges RTE's published forecast, but that series sits 1.1 GW below published consumption since 2023. Corrected for that bias, RTE wins (1.86% vs 2.18%).

chunks.title: WattCast: lesson, Retrain after a shock
chunks.text: A model trained on 2015-2021 and never updated over-forecasts 2023 by about 620 MW: the energy crisis changed consumption.

chunks.title: WattCast: lesson, History can't predict a lockdown
chunks.text: The 10 worst days of the backtest are all from the first COVID lockdown.

chunks.title: WattCast: limitations
chunks.text: The backtest uses observed temperatures; realistic forecast error adds about half a point of error. National level, temperature only: no wind, sunshine or cloud cover.

chunks.title: ThreatScope: overview
chunks.text: Detects network intrusions and explains every alert, with a response playbook. Evaluated on 17 attack types that never appear in its training data. Attacks caught: 84% in training conditions (attack types seen in training), 56.8% on match day (attack types never seen before). Stack: LightGBM, Autoencoder, SHAP, FastAPI, Streamlit. Demo: https://threatscope.medouaishamdi.com. Code: https://github.com/medouaishamdi/threatscope.

chunks.title: ThreatScope: problem and approach
chunks.text: Intrusion-detection demos often report 99% accuracy by testing on the same attack types they were trained on. Real attackers don't follow those rules. ThreatScope is evaluated on the NSL-KDD test set, which contains 3,750 connections from 17 attack types absent from training. Two detectors: a supervised LightGBM model for known attacks, and an autoencoder trained only on normal traffic that flags whatever it cannot reconstruct. Every threshold chosen on validation data, never on the test set. Each alert gets a severity, a SHAP explanation, the features the autoencoder found abnormal, a MITRE ATT&CK technique and a response playbook.

chunks.title: ThreatScope: lesson, Thresholds don't survive distribution shift
chunks.text: Tuned for 1% false alarms on validation data, the supervised model produced 8.1% on the test traffic. The autoencoder's threshold held.

chunks.title: ThreatScope: lesson, Some attacks are invisible
chunks.text: 77 test 'attacks' are byte-for-byte identical to normal connections. No model can catch them from these features, and the project says so.

chunks.title: ThreatScope: limitations
chunks.text: NSL-KDD is an old benchmark; modern traffic would need retraining on recent data. Connection-level features only: no payload inspection or correlation across hosts.

chunks.title: SentinelVision: overview
chunks.text: Detects and tracks people and vehicles in video, and raises alerts like hazard-zone intrusion. Runs in real time on a 2-core CPU, with no GPU and no cloud API. 25 FPS on a 2-core CPU, up to 1080p. Stack: YOLO11, ONNX Runtime, Kalman filter, FastAPI, Streamlit. Demo: https://sentinelvision.medouaishamdi.com. Code: https://github.com/medouaishamdi/sentinelvision.

chunks.title: SentinelVision: problem and approach
chunks.text: Camera systems in warehouses, shops and car parks produce hours of footage nobody watches. The useful part is a few events: someone entering a hazard zone, loitering, a vehicle stopped where it shouldn't be. YOLO11 detector exported to ONNX, with pre-processing and box decoding written by hand. A ByteTrack-style multi-object tracker (Kalman filter + Hungarian matching) to follow each person across frames. A rules engine for zone intrusion, loitering, line crossing, crowding and stopped vehicles, with events stored in SQLite. Annotated H.264 video, activity timeline and heatmap for every analysed clip.

chunks.title: SentinelVision: lesson, Reproduce the official number first
chunks.text: Matching the official mAP evaluator to within 0.003 proved the hand-written pre-processing and decoding were correct before building anything on top.

chunks.title: SentinelVision: lesson, Pick speed when it matters
chunks.text: YOLO11n is 2.4 times faster than YOLO11s for 6 points of mAP: the right trade for real time on a CPU.

chunks.title: SentinelVision: limitations
chunks.text: No re-identification: a person who leaves and comes back gets a new ID. COCO128 images come from COCO's training set, so absolute mAP is optimistic; it is used to verify the implementation.

chunks.title: DocuMind: overview
chunks.text: Ask questions about your own documents and get streamed answers that cite their sources. Benchmarked on questions phrased in the document's words and on paraphrases that share none of them. Right passage found first (keyword search): 95% in training conditions (questions using the document's words), 20% on match day (the same questions, paraphrased). Stack: Node.js, Express, Gemini API, BM25, Server-Sent Events. Demo: https://documind.medouaishamdi.com. Code: https://github.com/medouaishamdi/documind.

chunks.title: DocuMind: problem and approach
chunks.text: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) answers questions from your documents, but only as well as it retrieves the right passage. Keyword search misses paraphrases; embedding search misses exact codes and numbers. Hybrid retrieval: BM25 keyword search, implemented from scratch, fused with Gemini embeddings using Reciprocal Rank Fusion. Answers stream token by token with inline citations; a second model call checks how well each answer is supported by its sources. A benchmark of 40 labelled questions, half paraphrased, plus questions with no answer, to measure retrieval and refusals. Per-visitor rate limits and a daily budget so a public demo can't drain the API quota.

chunks.title: DocuMind: lesson, Measure before you claim
chunks.text: The keyword-only benchmark shows exactly why hybrid search is needed: near-perfect on the document's wording, and lost on paraphrases.

chunks.title: DocuMind: limitations
chunks.text: The benchmark is small (16 chunks), and the questions were written knowing the documents. Faithfulness is judged by a language model: an indicator, not ground truth.

chunks.title: DocuMind: DocuMind
chunks.text: A production-shaped RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) pipeline: upload documents, ask questions, get answers that are streamed live, cited back to their exact source passages, and automatically fact-checked against those sources. Free to run — Google's Gemini API, no credit card.

chunks.title: DocuMind: What it demonstrates
chunks.text: This isn't a ChatGPT wrapper. It's built around the parts of a real RAG system that actually matter in production: - Chunking with paragraph/sentence-aware boundaries (not blind character slicing) and overlap, so each chunk reads coherently as a standalone citation unit. - Asymmetric embeddings — documents are embedded with RETRIEVAL_DOCUMENT task type, queries with RETRIEVAL_QUERY , which is how Gemini's embedding model is actually trained to be used. - Semantic caching — repeated or paraphrased questions ("what's the refund window?" vs "how long do I have to get a refund?") are detected by comparing query embeddings, not exact string matches, and served instantly without a second model call. - Streaming responses over Server-Sent Events, so answers appear token-by-token instead of after a long wait. - Inline citations — the model is only allowed to answer from the numbered source excerpts it's given, and cites them like [1] , [2] inline; clicking a citation in the UI scrolls to that exact passage. - A faithfulness/hallucination check — after every answer, a

chunks.title: DocuMind: What it demonstrates
chunks.text: clicking a citation in the UI scrolls to that exact passage. - A faithfulness/hallucination check — after every answer, a second model call re-reads the answer against only the retrieved sources and scores how well-supported it actually is (0-100), flagging any unsupported claims. This is a lightweight, purpose-built version of what tools like Ragas measure. - Hybrid retrieval — every question is searched two ways: by meaning (Gemini embeddings) and by keywords (BM25, implemented from scratch in src/bm25.js ). The two rankings are merged with Reciprocal Rank Fusion. Embeddings understand paraphrases but miss exact tokens like error codes, product names and numbers; BM25 is the opposite. The mode can be switched per question ( hybrid , dense , bm25 ) to compare them. - A measured retrieval benchmark — npm run eval scores retrieval on a labelled question set (see Evaluation) instead of claiming it "works well". - Abuse protection for a public demo — per-IP sliding-window limits on questions (20/min) and uploads (5/min, the expensive embedding calls), Retry-After headers,

chunks.title: DocuMind: What it demonstrates
chunks.text: for a public demo — per-IP sliding-window limits on questions (20/min) and uploads (5/min, the expensive embedding calls), Retry-After headers, a memory sweep so the limiter can't grow forever, and an optional daily budget for the server's own API key , so visitors can't drain the free quota (people who paste their own key aren't counted). TRUST_PROXY=1 makes the limits work per visitor behind nginx/Caddy. - Tests — 22 tests ( npm test , Node's built-in runner, no extra dependencies) covering chunking, BM25, fusion, rate limits, the store and the full HTTP API with a fake model client, so they run offline in under a second.

chunks.title: DocuMind: Tech stack
chunks.text: - documind-api — Node.js + Express (plain JavaScript, no SDK dependency — talks to Gemini's REST API directly for embeddings, streaming generation, and the eval check). PDF text extraction via pdf-parse . The app is built by a factory ( createApp ) so the model client and the store can be swapped for fakes in tests. - documind-web — vanilla HTML/CSS/JS, no build step. Parses the SSE stream by hand (no library) to render live tokens, sources, and the eval badge.

chunks.title: DocuMind: An honest note on the vector store
chunks.text: This uses a JSON-file-backed store with cosine similarity computed in Node, not Pinecone/Milvus/pgvector. For a personal-scale app (hundreds to low thousands of chunks) this is genuinely fine and is mathematically the same operation those tools do — it just doesn't scale past what fits comfortably in memory. documind-api/src/store.js is where you'd swap in pgvector or a real vector DB; the rest of the API wouldn't need to change.

chunks.title: DocuMind: How it works, end to end
chunks.text: 1. Upload a .txt , .md , or .pdf file. The server extracts text, splits it into overlapping chunks, embeds each chunk (in batches), and stores them. 2. Ask a question. The question is embedded and checked against the semantic cache. On a miss, it is ranked against every chunk of the selected documents twice — cosine similarity of the embeddings and BM25 keyword scoring — and the two top-20 lists are fused (Reciprocal Rank Fusion) to keep the best 5. 3. Those 5 chunks are numbered and sent to the model with strict instructions: answer only from these sources, cite inline. 4. The answer streams back over SSE as it's generated. 5. Once complete, a second model call fact-checks the answer against only those same sources and returns a faithfulness score plus any unsupported claims. 6. The question, answer, sources, and eval result are cached (in memory) so a semantically similar future question skips regeneration entirely.

chunks.title: DocuMind: Evaluation
chunks.text: documind-api/eval/ holds a small benchmark: three original documents (an employee handbook, an e-bike manual and a privacy policy, all for fictional organisations, 16 chunks) and 40 labelled questions , each with the exact passage that answers it. Half are keyword questions that reuse the document's wording ("What does error E-07 mean?"). The other half are paraphrases that deliberately share no key terms with the answer ("How long until my bike is fully juiced up?" for "A full charge from empty takes about 4 hours 30 minutes"). Five extra questions have no answer in the documents, to check that the model refuses instead of inventing. A question counts as a hit@k when one of the top k retrieved chunks contains its evidence passage. The script uses the app's own chunker and retrieval code. BM25 alone (measured, no API key needed): Retrieval Questions Hit@1 Hit@3 Hit@5 MRR : : : : BM25 keyword (20) 95% 100% 100% 0.975 BM25 paraphrase (20) 20% 50% 55% 0.363 BM25 all (40) 57% 75% 78% 0.669

chunks.title: DocuMind: Evaluation
chunks.text: keyword (20) 95% 100% 100% 0.975 BM25 paraphrase (20) 20% 50% 55% 0.363 BM25 all (40) 57% 75% 78% 0.669 Keyword search is almost perfect when the user speaks the document's language and fails when they don't: that gap is why the app fuses it with embeddings. To measure dense and hybrid retrieval, and end-to-end answers, with your own key: Results are printed as tables and saved to eval/results.json , with per-question ranks. Limitations of this benchmark: - It is small: 16 chunks, so hit@5 is easy. Hit@1 and MRR are the informative numbers. - I wrote the questions myself, knowing the documents. - The faithfulness score comes from an LLM judge, so it is an indicator, not ground truth.

chunks.title: DocuMind: Running it publicly
chunks.text: The API reads its settings from documind-api/.env (see .env.example ). For a public demo: - set GEMINI_API_KEY so visitors can try it without a key; - set SERVER_KEY_DAILY_QUERIES (e.g. 200) so the free quota can't be drained; - set TRUST_PROXY=1 behind a reverse proxy; - serve documind-web/ as static files.

chunks.title: DocuMind: Notes / possible upgrades
chunks.text: - Swap the JSON store for pgvector or Pinecone once you outgrow in-memory search — the API surface stays the same. - The semantic cache is in-memory only and resets on restart; persist it the same way the document store is persisted if you want it to survive. - Add a cross-encoder re-ranker over the fused top-20 and measure it with npm run eval before keeping it.

chunks.title: HistoLens: HistoLens: colorectal tissue classification, tested on a different hospital
chunks.text: HistoLens classifies microscope images of colorectal cancer tissue (H&E-stained histology tiles) into 9 tissue types, including tumour , stroma , normal mucosa and lymphocytes. Most medical-imaging demos are tested on images from the same source as their training data. HistoLens is trained on one medical center's slides and tested on 7,180 tiles from a different clinical center , with different staining and scanning. That's the situation a real tool faces. Each prediction comes with: - a calibrated confidence ; - a "refer to a pathologist" flag when the model is unsure; - an occlusion map showing which part of the image the decision relied on. Research and portfolio project on public data. Not a medical device.

chunks.title: HistoLens: Results
chunks.text: Every model got the same training budget: 4 passes over 30,000 randomly drawn training images, on 2 CPU cores (no GPU). Model Parameters Same hospital (validation) Other hospital (test) Test macro F1 : : : : Small CNN, from scratch 1.2M 96.7% 95.4% 0.934 ResNet-18, from scratch 11.2M 93.7% 92.3% 0.890 ResNet-18, ImageNet-pretrained, no stain augmentation 11.2M 98.5% 95.1% 0.932 ResNet-18, ImageNet-pretrained + stain augmentation 11.2M 97.8% 95.7% 0.942

chunks.title: HistoLens: What I learned
chunks.text: 1. Validation accuracy picks the wrong model. Judged on same-hospital validation data, the best model is the pretrained ResNet-18 without stain augmentation (98.5%). On the other hospital it falls behind even the small CNN (95.1% vs 95.4%). Its 3.4-point drop is the price of learning one lab's colours. 2. Stain augmentation helps: a real but modest gain. H&E slides are stained with two dyes, and their intensity varies from lab to lab (see below). I implemented stain augmentation from scratch: - convert each training image to optical density; - separate the hematoxylin, eosin and residual stains (Ruifrok–Johnston colour deconvolution); - scale and shift each stain at random, then convert back. On the other hospital this fixes 171 tiles and breaks 124, for +0.6 points. McNemar's test gives p = 0.007 . It's one training run per model, so I'd want several seeds before claiming more. The test hospital's background tiles are dark purple, far outside the colour range the augmentation produces. Stronger augmentation, or stain normalization, would be the next

chunks.title: HistoLens: What I learned
chunks.text: are dark purple, far outside the colour range the augmentation produces. Stronger augmentation, or stain normalization, would be the next experiment. 3. Transfer learning matters when compute is limited. With the same small budget, ResNet-18 from scratch reaches only 92.3%, while starting from ImageNet weights gives 95.7%. Natural-image features (edges, textures) transfer to tissue. 4. Calibration tuned on one hospital doesn't transfer to another. Temperature scaling, the standard fix for over-confident networks, was fitted on validation data (T = 0.91). On the other hospital it made the calibration error slightly worse (0.7% → 1.2%). Both values are low, so the displayed confidence is trustworthy here. But only measuring on the other hospital could tell. 5. Referring uncertain tiles to a human pays off. Tiles the model answers Accuracy on those tiles : : 100% 95.7% 90% 98.7% 80% 99.5% The app refers a tile when its confidence is below 0.918, which keeps 90% of tiles. That threshold was read off the test hospital, so 98.7% is slightly optimistic for a

chunks.title: HistoLens: What I learned
chunks.text: which keeps 90% of tiles. That threshold was read off the test hospital, so 98.7% is slightly optimistic for a third hospital. 6. The hardest pair is smooth muscle vs cancer-associated stroma (11–14% confused with each other). Both are pink, fibrous, elongated tissue, and at 64×64 pixels they look alike.

chunks.title: HistoLens: How it's built
chunks.text: - Training: PyTorch with AdamW, a one-cycle learning-rate schedule, random 90° rotations and flips (tissue has no "up"), and stain plus brightness/contrast augmentation. Everything is in histolens/train.py . - Export: the final model is exported to ONNX , and the export is checked against PyTorch (max logit difference 7e-6). - Serving: the API and dashboard run on ONNX Runtime only . No PyTorch is needed to use the app, so installs are light and Docker images are small.

chunks.title: HistoLens: Data
chunks.text: PathMNIST from MedMNIST v2 (Yang et al., Scientific Data 2023), 64×64 version, CC BY 4.0. It is derived from: - training and validation: NCT-CRC-HE-100K, 100,000 tiles from 86 slides; - test: CRC-VAL-HE-7K, from a different clinical center. Both are from Kather et al., PLOS Medicine 2019.

chunks.title: HistoLens: Limitations
chunks.text: - Tiles, not patients. A clinical tool would analyse whole slides (thousands of tiles) and aggregate them per patient. - Low resolution. 64×64 pixels per tile, far below the full-resolution images pathologists look at. - Small scale. Only two medical centers, and one training run per model. - No out-of-distribution check. Anything uploaded gets one of the 9 labels: a random-noise image is called "Background" with 99% confidence. A real tool needs a reject option for non-tissue images. - Not a medical device. Not validated for diagnosis.

chunks.title: SentinelVision: SentinelVision: Real-Time Object Detection & Smart Surveillance
chunks.text: SentinelVision turns a camera feed into security and operations events . It detects people and vehicles, tracks them across frames, and applies rules: restricted-zone intrusion, loitering, directional line counting, crowding and stopped vehicles . Every event is logged with a snapshot, and you get an annotated video, an activity timeline and a heatmap. It runs faster than real time on a laptop CPU : no GPU, no PyTorch, no cloud API.

chunks.title: SentinelVision: Results
chunks.text: Detector accuracy (YOLO11n, COCO128) mAP50 0.671 / mAP50-95 0.504 (official evaluator: 0.674 / 0.505) Detector speed (2-core CPU, ONNX Runtime) 25 FPS for any input size up to 1080p Full pipeline (detect + track + rules + drawing) 1.2× to 2.1× faster than real time on the 5 test scenes People counting (hallway scene) 7/7 people counted, 4 west / 3 east: exact match with the manual count Tracking + rules cost < 1 ms per frame (inference is ~90% of the time) Model mAP50 mAP50-95 Person AP50 CPU FPS (720p) Size YOLO11n 0.671 0.504 0.785 24.9 10 MB YOLO11s 0.731 0.569 0.820 10.5 36 MB YOLO11n is the default: it's 2.4× faster for 6 points of mAP, which is the right trade-off for real time on a CPU. YOLO11s can be selected anywhere in the app. Why reproduce the official mAP? The pre-processing (letterbox), output decoding and non-maximum suppression are written by hand, not taken from a library. Matching the official evaluator to within 0.003 mAP proves the implementation

chunks.title: SentinelVision: Results
chunks.text: are written by hand, not taken from a library. Matching the official evaluator to within 0.003 mAP proves the implementation is correct. (YOLO11s is 0.012 lower because the official validator assigns multiple labels per box; I keep one label per box, as production inference does.) COCO128 images come from COCO train , so absolute mAP is optimistic. It's used here as a correctness check, not a benchmark claim.

chunks.title: SentinelVision: The 5 test scenes
chunks.text: Real surveillance-style footage from Intel's sample-videos (CC BY 4.0). Scene Rules What happens Warehouse (1080p) Hazard-zone intrusion, loitering, exit counting 3 workers cross into the taped hazard area: 3 critical alerts, 1 loitering Store aisles Dwell time per aisle, crowding Shoppers who stay over 15 s, crowd warnings when 5 people are in the aisle Parking lot Car lane + bike-path counting, stopped vehicles Bikes, pedestrians and cars counted by direction Hallway Two exit tripwires, group detection Exact people count per exit Office Restricted door area Each person entering the restricted area raises an alert Scene analysis Heatmap & timeline

chunks.title: SentinelVision: How it works
chunks.text: 1. Detection : YOLO11 exported once to ONNX, run with ONNX Runtime. Low confidence threshold (0.15): the tracker decides what's real. 2. Tracking : each object gets a constant-velocity Kalman filter . Detections are matched to tracks with the Hungarian algorithm on IoU in two passes : confident boxes first, then weak boxes to keep partly occluded people (the ByteTrack idea). New tracks need 3 hits before they get an ID, which removes one-frame false positives. 3. Rules run on each track's ground point (bottom-center of the box), the point that actually stands in a zone. Geometry is in normalized coordinates , so a configuration works at any resolution. 4. Frame skipping : a 60 FPS camera is analyzed at 10 FPS. The tracker bridges the gaps, which cuts compute by 6× with no loss for human-speed motion.

chunks.title: SentinelVision: Limitations & next steps
chunks.text: - Re-identification : someone who leaves and comes back gets a new ID (counts are per pass, not per unique person). Next step: an appearance embedding (e.g. OSNet) for re-ID. - Cyclists are detected as both a bicycle and a person; a rider-merging step would count them once. - Pretrained COCO classes only : safety-specific detection (helmets, vests) would need fine-tuning on a labelled dataset. - Zones are drawn per camera; perspective is not modelled (no real-world distances or speeds). - Evaluation of tracking uses one manually counted scene. A full benchmark would use MOT17 (HOTA/IDF1).

chunks.title: ThreatScope: ThreatScope: network intrusion detection that is tested on attacks it has never seen
chunks.text: Most intrusion-detection demos report 99% accuracy. They train and test on the same attack types . A real attacker does not follow those rules. ThreatScope is evaluated on the NSL-KDD test set, which contains 17 attack types that do not appear in training (3,750 connections). That is where the honest numbers come from. It combines two detectors: - Known-pattern model: LightGBM, trained on labelled attacks. It is strong on what it has seen and weak on new attacks. - Anomaly model: an autoencoder trained only on normal traffic . It flags whatever it cannot reconstruct, so it does not need to have seen an attack before. Every alert comes with: - a severity - an explanation (SHAP for the supervised model, per-feature reconstruction error for the autoencoder) - a MITRE ATT&CK technique - a response playbook

chunks.title: ThreatScope: Results (NSL-KDD test set, 22,544 connections)
chunks.text: Detector False alarms Known attacks caught Never-seen attacks caught ROC-AUC : : : : Supervised LightGBM 2.8% 76.7% 33.3% 0.966 Isolation Forest (normal-only) 1.0% 60.2% 41.3% 0.949 Autoencoder (normal-only) 1.3% 69.8% 53.4% 0.969 Hybrid (LightGBM OR autoencoder) 3.2% 84.0% 56.8% 0.967 The hybrid detects +70% more never-seen attacks than the supervised model (33% → 57%). The cost is +0.4 points of false alarms.

chunks.title: ThreatScope: What I learned (the interesting part)
chunks.text: 1. Thresholds don't survive distribution shift. I first set the supervised model's threshold to give 1% false alarms on a validation split. On the test traffic it produced 8.1% false alarms, eight times the budget. The NSL-KDD test set was recorded under different conditions from the training set. The autoencoder's threshold, learned on normal traffic only, stayed close to its budget (1.3%). That is why the final hybrid uses the default 0.5 threshold for LightGBM. The tuned version is kept in the table above as a documented failure. 2. At equal false-alarm rates, the anomaly model wins on new attacks. False-alarm rate Supervised: never-seen caught Autoencoder: never-seen caught : : : 1% 5% 42% 2% 5% 64% 5% 75% 79% 3. Leave-one-family-out: remove a whole attack family from training. Detection rate on that family (validation set): Family removed Supervised, family seen Supervised, family removed Hybrid, family removed : : : DoS 99.98% 61.4% 94.2% Probe 99.7% 26.2% 55.6% R2L 99.0% 1.0% 17.7% U2R (11 samples) 63.6% 0% 90.9% A supervised

chunks.title: ThreatScope: What I learned (the interesting part)
chunks.text: DoS 99.98% 61.4% 94.2% Probe 99.7% 26.2% 55.6% R2L 99.0% 1.0% 17.7% U2R (11 samples) 63.6% 0% 90.9% A supervised model essentially cannot detect a family it has not been taught. The anomaly model is what keeps coverage up. 4. Some attacks are invisible from these features. 77 test "attacks" are byte-for-byte identical to normal connections. These are mostly snmpgetattack , legitimate SNMP requests with a stolen community string. No model can catch them from connection statistics, and the README says so rather than hiding it. mailbomb and snmpguess are also missed: they look like normal mail and SNMP traffic. Per-attack recall is in reports/novel_attack_recall.csv .

chunks.title: ThreatScope: How it works
chunks.text: - No test-set tuning. Every threshold is chosen on a validation split of the training data. - Severity is critical, high or medium, from the supervised probability and the anomaly percentile. - The family guess is a hint, not a fact. On alerted test attacks it names the right family 62% of the time (54% on never-seen types), and the dashboard says so.

chunks.title: ThreatScope: Limitations
chunks.text: - The dataset is old. NSL-KDD (1999 traffic, cleaned in 2009) is a standard benchmark, but it is old. Modern attacks would need retraining on recent data such as CIC-IDS2017 or UNSW-NB15. The pipeline is dataset-agnostic as long as the features are tabular. - Connection-level features only. There is no payload inspection and no correlation across hosts or over time, so slow, distributed or content-based attacks are out of reach. - The false-alarm rate is per connection. 3.2% is still a lot of alerts on a busy network. In production you would aggregate alerts by source, and the operating-point slider shows the trade-off.

chunks.title: WattCast: WattCast: day-ahead forecasting of French electricity demand
chunks.text: WattCast forecasts France's national electricity consumption for each hour of tomorrow, the way the grid operator RTE does every day. It is built on 11 years of RTE eCO2mix data (2015 to June 2026) and hourly temperatures from five large French cities, weighted by population. It is backtested over 7.5 years : every year from 2019 to 2026 is forecast by a model trained only on the years before it, and compared hour by hour with RTE's own published forecasts .

chunks.title: WattCast: Results (every hour from January 2019 to June 2026)
chunks.text: Model MAPE Average error : : Same hour last week (baseline) 6.47% 3,496 MW Linear regression (baseline) 3.75% 1,878 MW WattCast (LightGBM) 2.18% 1,146 MW RTE's published day-ahead forecast 2.24% 1,140 MW RTE's forecast, bias-corrected (see below) 1.86% 946 MW Each forecast comes with an 80% prediction interval , which contains the actual value 79.5% of the time.

chunks.title: WattCast: Honest comparison with RTE
chunks.text: On paper, WattCast (2.18%) edges out RTE's published forecast (2.24%). That claim doesn't hold up, for two reasons: 1. The published RTE forecast has a definition gap. Since 2023, RTE's published forecast sits about 1.1 GW below published consumption every year, even for its same-day forecast. That points to a difference in what the two series measure, not to bad forecasting. Removing that bias, using only errors known at forecast time (a trailing 28-day average), brings RTE to 1.86% , better than WattCast. 2. The backtest uses observed temperatures, i.e. a perfect weather forecast. RTE has to use real weather forecasts. Adding a realistic 1.5 °C day-ahead temperature error raises WattCast's 2025 error from 1.89% to 2.40% . So RTE is better. That's expected: forecasting demand is a core job of the grid operator. Using public data only, WattCast comes within about 0.3 points of the bias-corrected RTE forecast with perfect weather, and roughly 0.8 points once realistic weather-forecast error is included. Year WattCast RTE published RTE bias-corrected Linear Last

chunks.title: WattCast: What I learned
chunks.text: 1. The 2022 energy crisis changed consumption, and a model that isn't retrained falls behind. After the crisis and the government's sobriété plan, France uses several GW less at the same temperature (see the heating curve below). A model trained on 2015–2021 and never updated over-forecasts 2023 by about 620 MW on average. Retraining every year cuts its error from 2.25% to 1.93%. 2. History can't predict a lockdown. The 10 worst days of the backtest are all from the first COVID lockdown (March–May 2020). WattCast was off by 11–16% on those days, while RTE stayed within 2–6%. A model that learns from consumption 2 and 7 days earlier needs days to catch up with a sudden break. RTE's forecast handled it far better, which suggests it was adjusted for the lockdown. 3. Prediction intervals must be calibrated. The raw 10%/90% quantile models covered only 64% of hours instead of 80%: they were over-confident on new data. Conformal calibration fixes this. I hold out the last year of training, measure

chunks.title: WattCast: What I learned
chunks.text: 80%: they were over-confident on new data. Conformal calibration fixes this. I hold out the last year of training, measure how much the interval must widen to cover 80% of it, and apply that margin. Coverage becomes 79.5% overall. It still varies by year: too narrow in 2022, the crisis year, and too wide in 2023. 4. France heats with electricity. On working days, every degree colder below about 14 °C adds ~2,200 MW (2015–2019) and ~2,100 MW (2023–2026). That's measured directly on the data, and in line with RTE's widely quoted figure of about 2,400 MW per °C. I first tried to get this number from the model ("what if tomorrow were 1 °C colder?") and got only ~1,000 MW per °C. That turned out to be a lesson about lag-based models: they anchor on recent real consumption, so a one-day change moves them much less than a lasting cold spell would.

chunks.title: WattCast: How it works
chunks.text: The forecast for day D is made on D-1, like RTE's day-ahead forecast, so only consumption up to D-2 is used. A test checks that changing consumption on D-1 or D leaves every feature of D unchanged. Features: - Calendar: hour, weekday, season, French public holidays, bridge days ( ponts ), August, Christmas break. - Temperature: population-weighted average of Paris, Lyon, Marseille, Lille and Bordeaux; 24 h and 72 h smoothing (buildings react with inertia); heating and cooling degrees; the day's min/max. - Recent consumption: 2 and 7 days earlier, the average of the previous week, and how much warmer or colder it is now than on those days. Models: - Baselines: same hour last week; a ridge regression. - WattCast: LightGBM (900 trees), plus 10% and 90% quantile LightGBM models for the conformally calibrated interval. - Backtest: an expanding window, retrained every year.

chunks.title: WattCast: Data
chunks.text: - RTE eCO2mix national data, "consolidated and definitive" (ODRE). Consumption every 30 min and RTE's forecasts every 15 min, both averaged to hourly. Licence Ouverte / Etalab. - Open-Meteo historical weather API. Hourly 2 m temperature (CC BY 4.0). To rebuild data/processed/hourly.parquet from scratch, save the raw files in data/raw/ as eco2mix-national-cons-def.csv and weather_ .csv , then run python -m wattcast.data .

chunks.title: WattCast: Limitations
chunks.text: - Observed, not forecast, temperatures. The backtest uses observed temperatures; the realistic cost of that is measured above (+0.5 points of error). - Temperature only. National level, with no other weather: wind chill, sunshine and cloud cover all affect demand too. - Blind to exceptional events (strikes, lockdowns, extreme cold-weather alerts) until they show up in recent consumption. - Approximate city weights. The population weights are rounded metropolitan populations; RTE uses its own national reference temperature, built from many more weather stations.

chunks.title: How this site works
chunks.text: Ouais FC is a 3D football game that serves as the portfolio. It is built with Three.js (WebGL), cannon-es physics and the Web Audio API; everything (world, sounds, music) is generated in code. The goalkeepers are run by Byte, a small online learner that counts where you shoot, blends it with a Markov chain over your previous shot, and dives where the next shot is most likely to go.
